The HTTP request/response cycle is the step‑by‑step exchange that starts when a browser asks for a URL and ends when the browser receives an HTML page (or other data) back from the server.  

When you type a URL such as `https://domain.com/blog/33/`, the browser sends an HTTP request to the web server, which first receives the request and then hands it to Django [1]. Django scans the URL‑pattern list in order, stops at the first match, creates an **HttpRequest** object and passes it to the view that corresponds to that pattern [2]. The view processes the request—e.g., looks up the blog post with ID 33—and returns an **HttpResponse** object containing the rendered page [2]. In a production setup the request travels through NGINX, then uWSGI, then Django, and the response follows the same path back to the client [3].  

**Worked example:** Requesting `/blog/1/` (the detail view of a post) triggers the URL matcher, calls the post‑detail view, which builds an HttpResponse with the post’s HTML and sends it back through the same chain, so the browser finally displays the post page [4][1].  

**Common mistake:** Many learners think Django can push data to the browser without a new request, but the framework only sends data in direct response to an incoming HTTP request; there is no built‑in mechanism for an open, server‑initiated connection [2].
